questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with fevers and a swollen right eyelid with a red eye, purulent drainage, tearing, and some blurriness. She was normally well and did not take any regular medications. She had no known drug allergies. She reported contact with a person that had recent smallpox vaccination as he had just joined the military. On exam, she had periorbital edema and redness on the right eyelid with a cutaneous vesicle present. She had visual acuity of 20/40 on the right. There was no inflammation of the cornea. Right submandibular and preauricular lymphadenopathy were also present. Conjunctival scrapings were sent for microbiology.
questions.lead_in: What is the best treatment option?
questions.explanation: Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine The patient has vaccine-associated preseptal cellulitis and conjunctivitis from contact with the military recruit who had recent smallpox immunization. It is important to remember that patients who receive smallpox vaccination may shed live virus while the vaccination site is healing. This typically lasts until separation of the scab which is usually 2–3 weeks after the vaccination. Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine are the treatment of choice. More severe cases warrant immunoglobulin, and it does help decrease shedding of virus. While vancomycin and a cephalosporin would be reasonable for the preseptal cellulitis, it would not address the conjunctivitis in this case. The vesicle points toward a viral etiology. Azithromycin would be for suspected Chlamydia; however, the clinical scenario is not consistent with such given the vesicle and recent contact with a contact of a recently vaccinated person.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q10

questions.question: A sheep farmer presents with a lesion on the fingers. [image-based question: EM of pox virus shown]
questions.question_raw: Lesion on the fingers of a sheep farmer. [image-based question: EM of pox virus shown]

parts.text: How would you treat this patient?

parts_raw.text: How would you treat this patient?

questions.model_answer:
a) Orf (contagious ecthyma), a parapoxvirus infection acquired from sheep/goats; the electron micrograph shows the characteristic ovoid parapoxvirus particle, and diagnosis is usually clinical based on exposure history plus a characteristic lesion (parapoxvirus/orf PCR or negative-stain EM of lesion material can confirm).

b) Supportive care only — the disease is self-limited, with complete healing in 4 to 6 weeks; keep the lesion covered, advise against autoinoculation and spread to contacts and animals, and treat any secondary bacterial infection. For large, giant, or granulomatous lesions (especially in immunocompromised hosts), options are surgical removal, topical 3% cidofovir cream, or topical imiquimod, all based on anecdotal reports without controlled trials.

How long would you tell him it would be until things resolved?
What treatment, if any, is required?

questions.model_answer:
a) Orf (contagious ecthyma) due to orf virus, a parapoxvirus acquired from sheep and goats; diagnosed clinically from exposure history plus the characteristic nodular lesion.

b) Short: 3 to 5 days.

c) Complete healing takes about 4 to 6 weeks from onset — macule/papule with target appearance days 7 to 14, ulceration at 14 to 21 days (acute stage), then regenerative papilloma and regression to normal epithelium. At three weeks he is mid-course; expect another 1 to 3 weeks.

d) None — the disease is self-limited; wound care, cover the lesion, avoid autoinoculation and transmission to contacts and animals. Reserve intervention for giant or granulomatous lesions (surgical excision; anecdotal topical 3% cidofovir or imiquimod), which occur more often in immunocompromised patients.
